targets.title: Incentives Build Robustness in BitTorrent
targets.authors: Bram Cohen
targets.venue: Workshop on Economics of Peer-to-Peer Systems (presented at IPTPS 2003)
targets.why_needed: The design document for BitTorrent's tit-for-tat choking algorithm: reciprocal upload allocation among the four best-uploading peers plus one optimistic unchoke slot, argued as approximating pareto-efficient exchange. Every attack paper in this domain (Piatek, Locher, Sirivianos, Levin) targets this exact mechanism, so its precise rule set is the baseline every exploit is measured against.

targets.title: Do Incentives Build Robustness in BitTorrent?
targets.authors: Michael Piatek, Tomas Isdal, Thomas E. Anderson, Arvind Krishnamurthy, Arun Venkataramani
targets.why_needed: Builds BitTyrant, a strategic client that reallocates upload toward peers with the best return-per-byte and reports a median 70% download-throughput gain on live swarms for a 1 Mbit/s connection; the paper this pass's own earlier draft cited from a secondary summary, so the primary text's exact experimental conditions (connection speed, swarm sample, measurement method) must be extracted directly rather than repeated from any prior document including this project's own CLAUDE.md.

targets.title: Free Riding in BitTorrent is Cheap
targets.authors: Thomas Locher, Patrick Moor, Stefan Schmid, Roger Wattenhofer
targets.why_needed: Introduces BitThief, a client that completes downloads while uploading nothing at all by exploiting optimistic unchoking and connecting to many more peers than the reference client does; the mechanism defeated (optimistic unchoke as the sole non-reciprocal admission path) is a specific, checkable property distinct from BitTyrant's exploit of the reciprocal-allocation formula.

targets.title: Free-riding in BitTorrent Networks with the Large View Exploit
targets.authors: Michael Sirivianos, Jong Han Park, Rex Chen, Xiaowei Yang
targets.why_needed: A third, independent free-riding construction against the same tit-for-tat mechanism, obtained by connecting to an inflated set of tracker-reported peers to raise the chance of receiving an optimistic unchoke; needed to check whether its measured completion rate and required peer-set size agree with or exceed BitThief's, since the brief requires presenting disagreeing numbers from independent papers side by side rather than picking one.

targets.title: BitTorrent is an Auction: Analyzing and Improving BitTorrent's Incentives
targets.authors: Dave Levin, Katrina LaCurts, Neil Spring, Bobby Bhattacharjee
targets.why_needed: Models the choking mechanism as a first-price auction, shows the model predicts measured behavior of deployed clients, and proposes PropShare, proportional-share upload allocation, as a replacement; needed as the measured comparison point against Cohen's original tit-for-tat rule and against BitTyrant's exploit, since PropShare is presented as a fix rather than only an attack.

targets.title: Free Riding on Gnutella
targets.authors: Eytan Adar, Bernardo A. Huberman
targets.why_needed: The original measurement establishing that a large share of Gnutella participants share no files while consuming search and download bandwidth from the rest, from a trace of actual client traffic; the number every later free-riding measurement paper positions itself against, and needed in full text since abstracts of this paper are known to be quoted with rounded or misattributed percentages elsewhere in this field's literature.

targets.title: Free Riding on Gnutella Revisited: The Bell Tolls?
targets.authors: Daniel Hughes, Geoff Coulson, James Walkerdine
targets.why_needed: An independent re-measurement of Gnutella free-riding five years after Adar and Huberman, needed to check whether the original fraction held, rose, or fell as the network and client population changed; this is the exact kind of independent-measurement paper the brief prioritizes because it is titled after its own contribution rather than the mechanism, making it easy to miss by keyword search alone.

targets.title: The Virtual Commons: Why Free-Riding Can Be Tolerated in File Sharing Networks
targets.authors: Ramayya Krishnan, Michael D. Smith, Zhulei Tang, Rahul Telang
targets.why_needed: An analytic model concluding that consumption-without-contribution does not collapse aggregate download performance below a stated bound under stated conditions on demand and peer population growth; this is a measured/derived structural claim to extract on its own terms, kept separate from the value judgment (common elsewhere in this literature) that free-riding is a defect to be engineered away regardless of its measured effect on throughput.

targets.title: KARMA: A Secure Economic Framework for Peer-to-Peer Resource Sharing
targets.authors: Vivek Vishnumurthy, Sangeeth Chandrakumar, Emin Gün Sirer
targets.venue: Workshop on Economics of Peer-to-Peer Systems (P2PEcon)
targets.why_needed: Defines a distributed scalar credit balance (karma) maintained by a replicated bank-set of nodes selected by consistent hashing over each participant's identifier, tolerant of a stated fraction of malicious bank-set members, increased on contribution and decreased on consumption; the currency/credit-scheme family member the brief names directly, and the account structure every later credit or token scheme in this domain is compared against.

targets.title: Samsara: Honor Among Thieves in Peer-to-Peer Storage
targets.authors: Landon P. Cox, Brian D. Noble
targets.why_needed: Enforces symmetric storage exchange without payment or certified identity by requiring each storage claimant to hold a matching claim from the peer it stores for, backed by forced periodic proof-of-possession challenges and a punitive reclamation mechanism when a peer holding a claim disappears; needed as the storage-specific incentive design distinct from a fungible credit system, and as the source of its measured proof-of-possession overhead and its stated failure condition when both peers in an exchange pair vanish simultaneously.

targets.title: Dandelion: Cooperative Content Distribution with Robust Incentives
targets.authors: Michael Sirivianos, Jong Han Park, Xiaowei Yang, Stanislaw Jarecki
targets.why_needed: Withholds the decryption key for a content block from a downloader until that downloader has itself uploaded a matching amount to others, stated by the authors to be provably non-manipulable unlike BitTorrent's choking heuristic; needed to extract the exact provable-non-manipulability claim and its assumption set, since it is cited elsewhere in this project only from a one-line paraphrase and the assumption set determines whether the same proof survives an open, identity-free membership model.

targets.title: Incentives for Sharing in Peer-to-Peer Networks
targets.authors: Philippe Golle, Kevin Leyton-Brown, Ilya Mironov
targets.why_needed: A game-theoretic model of a file-sharing network as a population of agents choosing a contribution level, deriving the Nash equilibria under a stated set of payoff structures and identifying which payoff structures make full free-riding the unique equilibrium; needed as the earliest formal mechanism-design treatment of consumption-without-contribution the brief asks for, giving the equilibrium-selection argument later empirical papers either confirm or contradict.

targets.title: Free-Riding and Whitewashing in Peer-to-Peer Systems
targets.authors: Michal Feldman, Christos H. Papadimitriou, John Chuang, Ion Stoica
targets.venue: IEEE Journal on Selected Areas in Communications
targets.why_needed: Formalizes whitewashing, discarding an identifier with a poor standing and rejoining under a fresh one, as a distinct failure mode from ordinary free-riding, and derives conditions under which a reciprocity mechanism remains incentive-compatible when identity is free to discard; this is the mechanism-design result that determines whether any credit or reputation scheme in this domain survives a Sybil-free but pseudonym-free membership model, which is exactly the membership model an identity-light decentralized system would use.

targets.title: Enforcing Fair Sharing of Peer-to-Peer Resources
targets.authors: Tsuen-Wan Ngan, Dan S. Wallach, Peter Druschel
targets.why_needed: A second, contemporaneous storage-fairness construction alongside Samsara, enforcing a global storage-consumption limit per participant via auditable, cryptographically linked storage claims distributed across the system rather than pairwise symmetric exchange; needed as the direct architectural alternative to Samsara so the comparison in the brief's per-component selection step (pairwise-symmetric versus globally-audited fairness) has both sides' measured overhead.

targets.title: BAR Fault Tolerance for Cooperative Services
targets.authors: Amitanand S. Aiyer, Lorenzo Alvisi, Allen Clement, Mike Dahlin, Jean-Philippe Martin, Carl Porth
targets.why_needed: Defines the Byzantine-Altruistic-Rational participant model, in which a protocol must be simultaneously safe against Byzantine participants and incentive-compatible against rational ones that deviate only when deviation is individually profitable, and gives a cooperative backup service built to that combined guarantee; needed because every incentive mechanism selected in this domain must be checked against this three-way model rather than against a Byzantine-only or rational-only threat model, which is a composition question the brief's cross-component conflict check is built to catch.

targets.title: A TorPath to TorCoin: Proof-of-Bandwidth Altcoins for Compensating Relays
targets.authors: Mainak Ghosh, Miles Richardson, Bryan Ford, Rob Jansen
targets.venue: Workshop on Hot Topics in Privacy Enhancing Technologies (HotPETs)
targets.why_needed: TorPath forms Tor circuits so that circuit participants can jointly measure end-to-end goodput on that specific circuit and collectively mine a currency unit (TorCoin) in proportion to the measured goodput, without a central bandwidth authority; this is the direct answer this domain must extract for whether goodput on a specific path, rather than a self-report, can back an incentive currency, and at what verification cost.

targets.title: From Onions to Shallots: Rewarding Tor Relays with TEARS
targets.authors: Rob Jansen, Andrew Miller, Paul Syverson, Bryan Ford
targets.venue: Workshop on Hot Topics in Privacy Enhancing Technologies (HotPETs)
targets.why_needed: A second bandwidth-reward currency proposed at the same workshop as TorCoin, using a trusted-directory-signed measurement rather than TorCoin's peer-measured circuit goodput; needed as the direct trust-model comparison point (trusted measurement authority versus peer measurement) for verifiable bandwidth accounting, one of the brief's named open problems for this domain.

targets.title: Proof-of-Work as Anonymous Micropayment: Rewarding a Tor Relay
targets.authors: Alex Biryukov, Ivan Pustogarov
targets.why_needed: A third relay-reward construction using client-side proof-of-work as the unit of payment instead of a measured-bandwidth currency, removing the need for any bandwidth measurement at all; needed to check whether replacing bandwidth verification with computational proof of work changes the security assumption from third-party bandwidth measurement to third-party-verifiable computation, and at what stated cost to the client.

targets.title: PeerFlow: Secure Load Balancing in Tor
targets.authors: Aaron Johnson, Rob Jansen, Nicholas Hopper, Aaron Segal, Paul Syverson
targets.why_needed: Shows that Tor's existing bandwidth-authority measurement (TorFlow) can be manipulated by a relay to gain disproportionate traffic share, gives the measured gain from the manipulation, and proposes a peer-measurement replacement bounded against that manipulation; needed as the direct evidence that a bandwidth-ordered or bandwidth-rewarded overlay's self-reported or centrally measured bandwidth is an attack surface, which is exactly HSkip+'s undefended honest-reporting assumption noted as an open problem in this project's brief.

targets.title: FlashFlow: A Secure Speed Test for Tor
targets.authors: Matthew Traudt, Rob Jansen, Aaron Johnson
targets.why_needed: Replaces the passive, slow-to-converge bandwidth measurement PeerFlow and TorFlow rely on with an active, adaptively-scheduled load test that a relay cannot inflate without also carrying the traffic, stating a measured convergence-time improvement over the prior measurement system; needed as the most recent (2021) advance in third-party bandwidth verification, checked against the 2024 result below for whether it has itself since been superseded.

targets.title: Proof of Backhaul: Trustfree Measurement of Broadband Bandwidth
targets.authors: Peiyao Sheng, Nikita Yadav, Vishal Sevani, Arun Babu, S. V. R. Anand, Himanshu Tyagi, Pramod Viswanath
targets.why_needed: A 2024 construction for a client to prove its own broadband backhaul bandwidth to a remote verifier without a trusted local measurement device, targeted directly at the brief's named open question of whether cheap third-party bandwidth verification exists; needed to determine whether this is a general answer to that question or specific to a broadband-access setting that does not transfer to a peer-to-peer overlay link.

targets.title: On the Accuracy of Tor Bandwidth Estimation
targets.authors: Rob Jansen, Aaron Johnson
targets.why_needed: An independent measurement of how accurately the deployed Tor bandwidth-measurement pipeline estimates the true capacity of a relay, using ground-truth data unavailable to the measurement system itself; this is the direct measured answer to the honest-reporting and verification-accuracy question the brief lists as open for capacity-ordered overlays, separate from any of the currency or reward-scheme proposals.

targets.title: Privacy Pass: Bypassing Internet Challenges Anonymously
targets.authors: Alex Davidson, Ian Goldberg, Nick Sullivan, George Tankersley, Filippo Valsorda
targets.why_needed: The deployed anonymous-rate-limiting-token construction the brief names directly: a client redeems one unlinkable, cryptographically blind-signed token per rate-limited action, obtained in a batch after passing one challenge, so the verifier can enforce a rate limit without learning which of a client's past challenge-passes corresponds to which later redemption; needed for its stated token-generation and redemption cost and its stated threat model limits (a verifier colluding with the issuer, or a client that shares tokens, are both out of scope as stated).

targets.title: Round-Optimal Password-Protected Secret Sharing and T-PAKE in the Password-Only Model
targets.authors: Stanislaw Jarecki, Aggelos Kiayias, Hugo Krawczyk
targets.why_needed: Defines the 2HashDH oblivious pseudorandom function construction later used as the cryptographic core of Privacy Pass's token issuance: the issuer computes a keyed function of a client-blinded input without learning the input, and the client unblinds the result into an unlinkable token; needed as the underlying primitive so the security assumption Privacy Pass rests on (discrete-log hardness of the issuer's key, one-more-unforgeability of the resulting function) is traceable to its proof rather than asserted secondhand.

targets.title: The Pythia PRF Service
targets.authors: Adam Everspaugh, Rahul Chatterjee, Samuel Scott, Ari Juels, Thomas Ristenpart
targets.why_needed: Deploys an oblivious pseudorandom function as a standalone rate-limiting network service: each client request is evaluated exactly once against a per-client counter enforced by the service, with the service unable to learn the client's input, and reports the achieved evaluation throughput and per-request latency; needed as the measured system-level cost of running an OPRF as a rate-limiting service rather than only as the cryptographic primitive inside a client protocol.

targets.title: A Fast and Simple Partially Oblivious PRF, with Applications
targets.authors: Nirvan Tyagi, Sofía Celi, Thomas Ristenpart, Nick Sullivan, Stefano Tessaro, Christopher A. Wood
targets.why_needed: Introduces the partially oblivious PRF (public metadata visible to both parties, private input still hidden) later standardized as the verifiable OPRF used in Privacy Pass's second protocol version, and states the measured evaluation-time improvement over the prior non-partially-oblivious construction it replaces; needed to determine what capability (per-issuer public metadata, meaning distinct rate-limit categories from a single key) the current deployed token scheme has that the original 2018 Privacy Pass construction lacked.

targets.title: Anonymous Tokens with Public Metadata and Applications to Private Contact Tracing
targets.authors: Ben Kreuter, Tancrède Lepoint, Michele Orrù, Mariana Raykova
targets.why_needed: A second, algebraic-MAC-based construction for a rate-limiting token that carries public metadata (a rate-limit category or trust tier visible on redemption), deployed in a production contact-tracing risk-score system; needed as the direct construction-family comparison against Tyagi et al.'s partially oblivious PRF approach for the same public-metadata capability, with each side's stated computational cost.

targets.title: Anonymous Counting Tokens
targets.authors: Fabrice Benhamouda, Mariana Raykova, Karn Seth
targets.why_needed: Generalizes anonymous rate-limiting tokens from a per-client global counter to a per-client-per-message counter, so an issuer can enforce that a client obtains at most one token for each distinct message while remaining unable to link a client's tokens across different messages; gives four constructions with stated tradeoffs and hardness assumptions (including one under q-DDHI and DCR). This is the 2023 advance the brief's retrieval instructions flag as necessary to check against any older, coarser-grained token scheme selected for this domain.

targets.title: WAKU-RLN-RELAY: Privacy-Preserving Peer-to-Peer Economic Spam Protection
targets.authors: Sanaz Taheri-Boshrooyeh, Oskar Thorén, Barry Whitehat, Wei Jie Koh, Onur Kilic, Kobi Gurkan
targets.why_needed: The direct academic treatment of the rate-limiting nullifier the brief names: each message carries a zero-knowledge proof of membership in a staked-deposit set plus a per-epoch nullifier derived from the sender's secret, so a second message in the same epoch reveals a linkable nullifier collision that lets any observer extract the sender's secret and forfeit its stake, without the honest sender's identity ever appearing on the wire; needed as the mechanism a client-side gossip network can use to rate-limit without any central issuer, at the stated cost of a staked deposit and a zero-knowledge proof per message.

targets.title: Message Latency in Waku Relay with Rate Limiting Nullifiers
targets.authors: Alvaro Revuelta, Sergei Tikhomirov, Aaryamann Challani, Hanno Cornelius, Simon Pierre Vivier
targets.why_needed: Measures the message-propagation latency added by attaching a rate-limiting-nullifier proof to every gossiped message in a deployed gossip-based relay network, using an analytical model, a single-host simulation at a stated node count, and a real multi-host deployment across stated geographic locations; this is the 2024 deployed-cost figure for the rate-limiting-nullifier mechanism the brief lists as an open area, needed with its exact node counts and topology rather than a rounded restatement.

targets.title: Stronger Key Derivation via Sequential Memory-Hard Functions
targets.authors: Colin Percival
targets.venue: BSDCan (self-published technical report; later standardized as RFC 7914)
targets.why_needed: Defines scrypt, a key-derivation function whose evaluation cost is dominated by filling and repeatedly re-reading a large pseudorandom array held in memory, so that building custom hardware to lower the per-evaluation time gains far less than it does against a purely computational function; the foundational memory-hard function the brief names, needed for its stated area-time tradeoff argument and its parameterization (memory size N, block size r, parallelization p).

targets.title: Argon2: New Generation of Memory-Hard Functions for Password Hashing and Other Applications
targets.authors: Alex Biryukov, Daniel Dinu, Dmitry Khovratovich
targets.venue: IEEE European Symposium on Security and Privacy (EuroS&P)
targets.why_needed: The winner of the Password Hashing Competition, giving two variants (data-dependent Argon2d and data-independent Argon2i) with a stated time-memory tradeoff resistance proof for each and measured throughput at stated memory and pass-count parameters; needed as the current reference memory-hard construction that any rate-limiting-without-identity design in this domain would use in place of the older scrypt, and for the specific tradeoff (Argon2d resists tradeoff attacks better but leaks memory-access patterns; Argon2i does not) that decides which variant a given threat model requires.

targets.title: Towards Practical Attacks on Argon2i and Balloon Hashing
targets.authors: Joël Alwen, Jeremiah Blocki
targets.venue: IEEE European Symposium on Security and Privacy (EuroS&P)
targets.why_needed: Gives a computed depth-reduction attack against the data-independent memory-hard functions (Argon2i, Balloon Hashing) at their standardized pass-count parameters, stating the achieved reduction in effective memory-hardness at those parameters; needed as the direct critique bounding how many passes a data-independent memory-hard function needs before its data-independence stops paying for the side-channel resistance it is chosen for.

targets.title: Balloon Hashing: A Memory-Hard Function Providing Provable Protection Against Sequential Attacks
targets.authors: Dan Boneh, Henry Corrigan-Gibbs, Stuart Schechter
targets.why_needed: A data-independent memory-hard function with a stated formal proof of memory-hardness against a sequential (non-parallel) evaluator, offered as a licensing-unencumbered alternative to Argon2 with a different construction (a stack of expander-graph-connected buffers rather than Argon2's data-dependent shuffling); needed as the construction Alwen and Blocki's 2017 attack above is stated against, so the attack's target and the construction's proof can be checked against each other directly.

targets.title: Client Puzzles: A Cryptographic Countermeasure Against Connection Depletion Attacks
targets.authors: Ari Juels, John Brainard
targets.why_needed: Defines an interactive challenge-response puzzle a server issues before committing a scarce resource to a connection request, with a stated property that the puzzle's difficulty can be scaled by the server in response to observed load without changing the protocol; needed as the interactive-puzzle branch of rate-limiting-without-identity, distinct from HashCash's non-interactive self-generated stamp, with its own cost and its own failure condition (a server under attack must still generate and track outstanding puzzles).

targets.title: Pricing via Processing or Combatting Junk Mail
targets.authors: Cynthia Dwork, Moni Naor
targets.why_needed: The originating paper for the idea underlying every proof-of-work rate limiter in this domain: a sender attaches to each request a value expensive to compute but cheap for the receiver to check, so the receiver can require one per request without maintaining any per-sender state or identity; needed to determine what the original paper actually proves about the cost gap between computing and checking, since HashCash and every rate-limiting proof-of-work scheme in this domain traces its security argument back to this construction.

targets.title: Hashcash - A Denial of Service Counter-Measure
targets.authors: Adam Back
targets.why_needed: The specific non-interactive proof-of-work stamp construction (a partial hash-collision search over a string carrying the resource, a timestamp, and a nonce) used as the HashCash rate limiter named directly in the brief, and reused inside the 4P protocol already in this project's evidence file as a per-request rate limiter against private-set-intersection enumeration; needed for its stated verification cost (one hash) against its stated generation cost (an expected number of hash attempts set by a leading-zero-bit count) so that cost ratio can be checked against later VDF-based alternatives.

targets.title: Verifiable Delay Functions
targets.authors: Dan Boneh, Joseph Bonneau, Benedikt Bünz, Ben Fisch
targets.why_needed: Defines a verifiable delay function: a computation that takes a stated minimum number of sequential steps even on unbounded parallel hardware, produces a unique output for a given input, and comes with a proof checkable far faster than the computation itself; unlike a memory-hard function or ordinary proof-of-work, a VDF's minimum-time property does not degrade under parallel or ASIC hardware, which the paper states directly and proves under a sequentiality conjecture on repeated squaring in a group of unknown order. Needed as the foundational primitive for rate limiting by elapsed real time rather than by consumed computation or memory, with its stated construction cost and its stated open problem (a plausible sequentiality assumption without a reduction to a standard hardness problem).

targets.title: Simple Verifiable Delay Functions
targets.authors: Krzysztof Pietrzak
targets.why_needed: An independent, concurrently developed verifiable delay function construction over the same repeated-squaring-in-an-unknown-order-group setting as Boneh, Bonneau, Bünz, and Fisch, with a different, interactive-turned-non-interactive proof of correctness; needed as the direct construction-level comparison (proof size, verifier computation) against the other 2018/2019 VDF constructions in this domain, since VDF deployments (Chia, Ethereum research) had to choose between this and Wesolowski's construction below on stated grounds.

targets.title: Efficient Verifiable Delay Functions
targets.authors: Benjamin Wesolowski
targets.why_needed: A third repeated-squaring-based verifiable delay function construction with a stated constant-size proof and stated constant verifier time independent of the delay parameter, the two properties on which it is preferred over Pietrzak's construction in deployed systems; needed with its exact stated proof size and verification cost so the tradeoff against Pietrzak's larger but simpler-to-generate proof is a cited comparison rather than an assumed one.
